title: ThermosClear
question: How does a thermos work?
hook: A steel flask keeps chai hot from breakfast to teatime with nothing at all: a gap emptied of air, two mirror-bright walls and a good stopper. Block heat's three escape routes in 3D, run twelve hours in twenty seconds, and find out why a fizzy drink should never go in one.

explainer.title: A bottle inside a bottle
explainer.text: A vacuum flask is two bottles, one inside the other, joined only in a thin ring at the neck. The air between them has been pumped out, the facing walls are shiny, and a stopper closes the mouth. All-steel flasks weld two steel bottles together; older ones hold a silvered glass refill in a case.

explainer.title: Three escapes, three blocks
explainer.text: Heat leaves by conduction, convection and radiation. The vacuum stops the first two: with the 5 mm gap full of air, 90 °C chai would lose about 12 W by conduction, and with a vacuum only hundredths of a watt. Radiation crosses a vacuum, so the walls are shiny: dull walls would leak about 15 W, polished steel about 0.7 W.

explainer.title: The real leaks: neck and stopper
explainer.text: Where the vacuum can't reach, heat still gets out: along the neck, where the walls are joined, and through the stopper. In a good 500 mL steel flask they carry over half of the roughly 2 W it loses at 90 °C.

explainer.title: Slow cooling, not no cooling
explainer.text: A flask cools along the same curve as any hot drink, about twenty times more slowly than a jug with a lid. Started at 95 °C in a 20 °C room, a good steel flask is near 75 °C after 6 hours and 60 to 65 °C after 12. Half-full, it cools about twice as fast.

explainer.title: Making and losing the vacuum
explainer.text: Removing half the air does nothing: conduction only falls once the gas is so thin that molecules cross the gap without meeting, below about 1 pascal. Steel flasks are sealed in a vacuum furnace with a getter to soak up stray hydrogen. If the outside of a flask gets warm, the vacuum has gone.

explainer.title: Use it safely
explainer.text: Hot drinks in a flask stay hot enough to scald for hours. Never seal in a fizzy or fermenting drink: its gas can push on a 4 cm stopper like a weight of tens of kilograms. Food kept warm should stay above 60 °C, as the WHO advises.

concepts.def: A double-walled bottle with the air pumped out of the gap between the walls. Often called a thermos, a former trademark that became an everyday word.
Heat passed on by molecules bumping into their neighbours. A vacuum has almost none to pass it on.
Heat carried by infrared light, which crosses a vacuum. Shiny walls block it.
How strongly a surface glows in the infrared, from 0 to 1: about 0.03 for silvered glass, 0.075 for polished steel, 0.9 for a dull surface.
How far a gas molecule travels before hitting another. In a good flask's gap it is longer than the gap itself.
Heat flows out at a rate proportional to the temperature difference, so hot things cool fast at first and then slower.
Heat stored divided by heat lost per degree: about 20 hours for a good 500 mL steel flask, under an hour for a jug.
A reactive metal sealed into a vacuum to soak up gas that seeps out of the walls later.
About 5 to 60 °C, where germs in food multiply fastest. The WHO advises keeping cooked food above 60 °C.
